newsitem.title: USA: Access Health plunges on lower earnings forecast.
newsitem.headline: Access Health plunges on lower earnings forecast.

text.p: Health care services provider Access Health Inc. lost nearly a third of its market value Wednesday after it said it expected its fiscal 1997 earnings to fall as much as 17 percent below analysts' estimates.
Shares in Access Health, which is based in Rancho Cordova, Calif., plunged by $7.125 to $14.375 on the Nasdaq market, where it was one of the most actively traded issues.

The company said after the stock market closed on Tuesday that it believed its fiscal 1997 earnings would be between 15 cents and 17 cents below the consensus estimate of 99 cents a share. However, it said it expected sales and earnings in 1998 to grow by at least 35 percent.
For the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, Access reported net income of $8.13 million, or 61 cents a share.
Access, which contracts personal health care management services to employers and health care providers, cited slower enrollment growth and competitive pricing for the revised outlook.
It said the slowdown was a direct consequence of the cost pressures facing health maintenance organisations (HMOs), which were increasingly cautious about investing in new services.

"This is a transition year for large health care plans," said Matt Plavan, director of investor relations. "More of them are saying to us, 'Can you show me the return on our investment?'" Plavan said two years ago the same health plans were aggressively adding new services as a way to retain customers.

Access' services include health information, prevention and care management programmes that are available over the Internet, on cable television and through 24-hour telephone access to triage nurses who provide referral services.

Plavan said Access still believes its services are one of the best ways for health plans to control costs since its network is broader than what most individual plans could reasonably offer on their own.
"We are still showing a very strong growth rate and we feel we are being conservative today saying we see 35 percent growth in 1998," Plavan said.
